claims.text: The initial composite contains W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
The initial composite contains Ti-rich interdendritic channels.
Ti-rich interdendritic channels contribute to phase separation and interfacial void formation.
Liquid-metal dealloying in molten Cu can selectively remove Ti-rich interdendritic channels.
Selective removal of the Ti-rich channels will produce an aligned, RHEA-like Cu composite structure.
The dealloyed structure will provide more continuous bonding between W and Cu.
More continuous W–Cu bonding will reduce interfacial void formation.
Removing Ti-rich regions will reduce phase separation.
Selective dealloying will create a more homogeneous and continuous composite microstructure.
A more homogeneous and continuous microstructure will enhance thermal conductivity.
The conductivity enhancement will persist under irradiation and cyclic thermal loading.
The treated composite will have higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite.
The treated composite will show less interfacial voiding than the untreated composite.
The treated composite will show less phase separation than the untreated composite.
The untreated W–Cu composite has significant phase separation and interfacial void formation.
Phase separation and interfacial void formation cause the untreated composite to have inferior thermal conductivity.
Molten-Cu dealloying can be controlled to remove Ti-rich phases without damaging the W and Cu structures.
The proposed benefit is applicable under thermal and irradiation conditions typical of W plasma-facing material to Cu cooling-component joints.
